figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of the framework. A human screenplay is corrupted into a condensed story outline (corruption). The script agent reconstructs the screenplay from the outline with the help of the skill library (reconstruction); a loss agent contrasts the reconstruction against the human original to produce a textual loss; a backward agent routes this loss into the skill library as fine-grained updates. The reconstruction loop iterates to continue to improve reconstruction quality (loop). The same corruption-reconstruction-loop framework applies to any domain beyond screenplay that offers human reference artifacts like theorem proving or research writing.
figures.headline: Reconstructing screenplays from outlines lets a loss agent feed textual gaps back into the skill library in a loop.
citing_sentences: Our framework treats a skill library as the trainable parameters of the agent, optimizing it through a corruption-and-reconstruction loop as illustrated in Figure 1.

figures.caption: Backward credit assignment with memory regularization and MoE routing. Loss reports are reduced into summaries (left), processed by serialized micro-steps (center), and routed into expert folders with a linter enforcing token limits (right).

abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle in highly specialized domains. Rather than parameter-level adaptation of LLMs which is costly and difficult to interpret, external skills (often defined as text files) have been recently proposed to augment LLMs for specialized domains. However, such skills rely on costly active human annotations or passive summarization of high-quality examples. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised approach for agent self-evolution that learns domain-specific skills directly from existing high-quality human artifacts, without additional human annotations or external rewards. Inspired by diffusion models, our approach follows a forward–loss–backward process to reconstruct human artifacts by iteratively learning the agent’s external skill library rather than updating its model parameters. Experiments on short-drama screenwriting demonstrate that our approach enables agents to autonomously extract generalizable writing skills from human-authored scripts and substantially improve domain-specific generation quality. Our approach provides a scalable paradigm for agents to continuously learn many kinds of complex skills from existing high-quality human artifacts.

sections.body: The section argues that LLMs often underperform human experts in specialized domains. It states that fine-tuning is impractical because the strongest models are closed-source and fine-tuning is expensive, risks catastrophic forgetting, and ties learned behavior to one checkpoint. External skills are presented as portable and human-auditable, but existing skill libraries depend on manual expert creation. The authors propose a self-supervised framework that trains an external skill library rather than model weights, using high-quality human artifacts as supervision without additional human feedback or external rewards. Stated contributions are the framework, validation on short-drama screenwriting where verifiable rewards are unavailable, ten event-based metrics designed with professional practitioners, and released code.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly and opaque, and hand-written skills are a bottleneck, motivating self-supervised skill acquisition.

sections.body: Existing ways to build skill libraries include expert-written skills, distillation of agent trajectories, and direct summarization of high-quality examples. Trajectory-based methods require successful runs, which are hard to judge in open-ended domains such as screenwriting. The authors follow direct summarization but add a corruption-and-reconstruction learning signal borrowed from diffusion models: a human artifact is corrupted into a summary, the agent reconstructs the original, and learning comes from the gap between the two. For organization, the paper adopts Mixture-of-Experts routing so that skills stay localized. For updating, it follows textual-gradient work, routing textual losses to relevant skills while model parameters stay frozen.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior skill methods need costly human writing or successful trajectories, so the authors summarize and reconstruct high-quality examples instead.

sections.body:
The method corrupts each professional screenplay episode into a condensed story outline, then has a script agent reconstruct the episode with help from rule cards it reads, logging which cards were activated.

- A loss agent compares the reconstruction with the human original and writes a dense semantic loss report.
- A backward agent assigns credit to cards, with four operations: strengthen, narrow, create, and merge.
- A rule linter caps each card body at 1,200 tokens and each description at 200 tokens, which the authors say stops cards from becoming incident logs; before the linter, the longest card had grown to 2,500 lines.
- Backward updates run in serialized micro-steps, because processing all loss reports at once caused vague edits.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A corruption-and-reconstruction loop trains a skill library, with capacity limits and micro-step updates to keep it organized.

sections.body: Training uses twenty professionally written short-drama stories, each with 49 to 70 episodes of roughly 2,000 characters, over three epochs with a 1,200-token-per-card limit. The main model is Claude Sonnet 4.6, and the training loop is also tested with Kimi K2.6 and Claude Opus 4.8. Six held-out stories, totaling 385 episodes, are generated under four configurations with the same execution context budget: Base with an empty skill library, +Few-shot with human-written scripts as examples, +Distill with rules learned directly from human originals, and +Ours with the reconstruction loop. Line-level style metrics come from a rule-based parser, and episode-level structure metrics are judged by an LLM with quoted evidence. The supplied section text does not include the resulting scores.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Held-out evaluation compares four configurations across 385 episodes from six unseen stories using ten metrics.
